amc12-ahsme-1970-01.title: Work from the inside
amc12-ahsme-1970-01.body:
$\sqrt1=1$, $\sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt2$, so the number is $\sqrt{1+\sqrt2}$. Its fourth power is $(1+\sqrt2)^2=3+2\sqrt2$.

**Answer: (E) $3+2\sqrt{2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1970-02.title: Common perimeter
amc12-ahsme-1970-02.body:
Let the perimeter be $4$: square side 1, area 1; circle radius $\frac2\pi$, area $\pi\cdot\frac4{\pi^2}=\frac4\pi$. Ratio $\frac4\pi$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{4}{\pi}$**

amc12-ahsme-1970-02.title: Sanity check
amc12-ahsme-1970-02.body:
For a fixed perimeter the circle encloses the most area, so the ratio must exceed 1: only $\frac4\pi\approx1.27$ and $4$ qualify, and $4$ is far too big.

**Answer: (A)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-04.title: Simplify the sum
amc12-ahsme-1970-04.body:
$(n-1)^2+n^2+(n+1)^2=3n^2+2$, which leaves remainder 2 when divided by 3 — never divisible by 3. For 11: $n=5$ gives $16+25+36=77=7\cdot11$. (This also shows (D) is false; $n=1$ gives $5$, so (C) is false; $n=0$ gives $2$, so (A) is false.)

**Answer: (B)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-06.title: Vertex
amc12-ahsme-1970-06.body:
The vertex of $y=x^2+8x$ is at $x=-\frac82=-4$, where $y=16-32=-16$.

**Answer: (B)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-07.title: Equilateral triangle
amc12-ahsme-1970-07.body:
$XA=XB=AB=s$, so $ABX$ is equilateral and $X$ is $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}s$ from $AB$. The distance to $CD$ is $s-\frac{\sqrt3}2s=\frac12s(2-\sqrt3)$.

**Answer: (E)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-11.title: Vieta
amc12-ahsme-1970-11.body:
The third root $r$: sum of roots $-2+1+r=0$ (no $x^2$ term), so $r=1$. Then $2x^3-hx+k=2(x+2)(x-1)^2=2x^3-6x+4$: $h=6,k=4$, $|2h-3k|=0$.

**Answer: (E)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-12.title: Coordinates
amc12-ahsme-1970-12.body:
Tangent to the opposite sides $AB$ and $CD$ means $AD=2r$. Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(w,0)$, $D=(0,2r)$; the centre is $(r,r)$. The midpoint of $AC$ is $(\frac w2,r)$, at distance $\frac w2-r=r$ from the centre, so $w=4r$. Area $4r\cdot2r=8r^2$.

**Answer: (C) $8r^2$**

amc12-ahsme-1970-12.title: Symmetry
amc12-ahsme-1970-12.body:
The midpoint of $AC$ is the centre of the rectangle, on the horizontal midline — the same line as the circle's centre. So the rectangle's centre is $2r$ from side $AD$ (one radius to the circle's centre, one more to the circle), giving length $4r$ and width $2r$.

**Answer: (C)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-14.title: Difference of roots
amc12-ahsme-1970-14.body:
The roots differ by $\sqrt{p^2-4q}$. Setting this to 1: $p^2=4q+1$, and $p>0$ gives $p=\sqrt{4q+1}$.

**Answer: (A)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-15.title: Find the trisection points
amc12-ahsme-1970-15.body:
The step is $\frac13(9,-6)=(3,-2)$, so the trisection points are $(-1,3)$ and $(2,1)$. The line through $(3,4)$ and $(-1,3)$ has slope $\frac14$: $4(y-4)=x-3$, i.e. $x-4y+13=0$.

**Answer: (E)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-17.title: Counterexamples
amc12-ahsme-1970-17.body:
$pr>qr$ forces $r>0$ and $p>q$. Then $-p<-q$, so (A) is false. With $p=1,q=-5$: (B) $-1>-5$ holds but (C) $1>5$ fails. With $p=2,q=1$: (B) $-2>1$ fails and (D) $1<\frac12$ fails. None always holds.

**Answer: (E)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-20.title: Project the midpoint
amc12-ahsme-1970-20.body:
$H$ and $K$ are the feet of perpendiculars from $B$ and $C$ to line $HK$. The foot $N$ of the perpendicular from $M$ is the midpoint of $HK$ (projection preserves midpoints). So $M$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $HK$, and $MH=MK$ always.

**Answer: (A)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-21.title: Revolutions
amc12-ahsme-1970-21.body:
The odometer counts wheel turns assuming radius 15. The route is 450 miles (read with the correct radius). On the way back the wheels made fewer turns, in ratio $\frac{440}{450}$, so the new radius is $15\cdot\frac{450}{440}=15.341$ inches, an increase of about $0.34$ inch.

**Answer: (B) .34**

amc12-ahsme-1970-22.title: Notice the pattern
amc12-ahsme-1970-22.body:
The sum of $n+1,\dots,3n$ is $2n\cdot\frac{(n+1)+3n}{2}=n(4n+1)$, and $\frac{4n(4n+1)}{2}=2n(4n+1)$ is exactly twice that: $300$.

**Answer: (A)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-23.title: Prime factorisation
amc12-ahsme-1970-23.body:
$10!=2^8\cdot3^4\cdot5^2\cdot7$ and $12=2^2\cdot3$. The largest $k$ with $12^k\mid10!$: $2k\le8$ and $k\le4$, so $k=4$.

**Answer: (D) 4**

amc12-ahsme-1970-24.title: Small triangles
amc12-ahsme-1970-24.body:
If the hexagon has side $t$, the triangle has side $2t$. The triangle splits into 4 equilateral triangles of side $t$; the hexagon into 6. So the hexagon's area is $\frac64\cdot2=3$.

**Answer: (B) 3**

amc12-ahsme-1970-25.title: Ceiling via floor
amc12-ahsme-1970-25.body:
The number of ounces charged is $W$ rounded up, $\lceil W\rceil=-[-W]$. Cost $-6[-W]$. Note (D) fails for whole numbers: $W=2$ costs 12, not 18.

**Answer: (E)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-26.title: All four lines are concurrent
amc12-ahsme-1970-26.body:
$x+y=5$ and $x-y=-1$ meet at $(2,3)$. Check the others: $2\cdot2-3\cdot3+5=0$ ✓ and $3\cdot2+2\cdot3-12=0$ ✓. All four lines pass through $(2,3)$, and each intersection of a line from the first pair with a line from the second pair is this point. One point.

**Answer: (B) 1**

amc12-ahsme-1970-27.title: Example
amc12-ahsme-1970-27.body:
The 6-8-10 triangle has area 24 and perimeter 24; its inradius is $\frac{6+8-10}{2}=2$.

**Answer: (A)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-28.title: Coordinates at the centroid
amc12-ahsme-1970-28.body:
Put the centroid $G$ at the origin with $A=(2a,0)$, $B=(0,2b)$ along the perpendicular medians. Then the midpoint of $BC$ is $(-a,0)$, so $C=(-2a,-2b)$. Now $AC^2=16a^2+4b^2=36$ and $BC^2=4a^2+16b^2=49$. Adding: $20(a^2+b^2)=85$, so $AB^2=4(a^2+b^2)=17$.

**Answer: (A) $\sqrt{17}$**

amc12-ahsme-1970-29.title: Angles from 12
amc12-ahsme-1970-29.body:
Now $10{:}t$. In 6 minutes the minute hand is at $6(t+6)^\circ$. Three minutes ago the hour hand was at $300+\frac12(t-3)$ degrees. Opposite: $300+\frac{t-3}{2}-6(t+6)=180$, so $5.5t=82.5$, $t=15$.

**Answer: (D) 10:15**

amc12-ahsme-1970-29.title: Check
amc12-ahsme-1970-29.body:
At 10:21 the minute hand is at $126^\circ$; at 10:12 the hour hand was at $306^\circ$. They differ by $180^\circ$ ✓.

**Answer: (D)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-30.title: Cut off a parallelogram
amc12-ahsme-1970-30.body:
Draw through $D$ a line parallel to $BC$, meeting $AB$ at $E$. Then $EBCD$ is a parallelogram: $EB=CD=b$ and $\angle EDC=\angle B$. So $\angle ADE=\angle D-\angle B=\angle B$. Also $\angle AED=\angle B$ (corresponding angles, $DE\parallel CB$). So triangle $AED$ is isosceles with $AE=AD=a$, and $AB=AE+EB=a+b$.

**Answer: (E) $a+b$**

amc12-ahsme-1970-30.title: Special case
amc12-ahsme-1970-30.body:
Take $\angle B=45^\circ$ and $\angle D=90^\circ$. Since $AB\parallel CD$, $\angle A=180^\circ-\angle D=90^\circ$, so $ABCD$ is a right trapezoid with height $AD=a$. Side $BC$ makes a $45^\circ$ angle with $AB$, so it extends $AB$ beyond $CD$ by exactly the height $a$: $AB=b+a$. Among the choices only (E) gives $a+b$ for all $a,b$ in this case.

**Answer: (E)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-31.title: Count by the digit deficit
amc12-ahsme-1970-31.body:
The digits fall short of 45 by 2: either one digit is 7 (5 numbers) or two digits are 8 (10 numbers) — 15 numbers.

Divisible by 11 means $d_1-d_2+d_3-d_4+d_5\equiv0\pmod{11}$. For 99999 this is 9. Lowering odd-place digits decreases it, lowering even-place digits increases it, by a total of 2. Only $9+2=11$ works, so both units of deficit must be in places 2 and 4: $97999$, $99979$, $98989$. Probability $\frac3{15}=\frac15$.

**Answer: (B) 1/5**

amc12-ahsme-1970-32.title: Combined distances
amc12-ahsme-1970-32.body:
Let the circumference be $C$. At the first meeting they have together covered $\frac C2$; at the second, $\frac{3C}{2}$, i.e. three times as much. So $B$ has gone $300$, and $A$ has gone $3\left(\frac C2-100\right)$. Also $A$ has gone $C-60$. So $\frac{3C}{2}-300=C-60$, $C=480$.

**Answer: (C) 480**

amc12-ahsme-1970-32.title: Check
amc12-ahsme-1970-32.body:
$C=480$: first meeting $B$ 100, $A$ 140 (sum 240 = half lap). Second meeting $B$ 300, $A$ 420 = $480-60$ ✓.

**Answer: (C)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-33.title: Digit frequency
amc12-ahsme-1970-33.body:
Write $0,\dots,9999$ with four digits (leading zeros). Each position shows each digit 1000 times, so the digit sum is $4\cdot1000\cdot45=180{,}000$. Adding 1 for $10000$: $180{,}001$.

**Answer: (A) 180,001**

amc12-ahsme-1970-33.title: Pairing
amc12-ahsme-1970-33.body:
Pair $n$ with $9999-n$ for $0\le n\le9999$: digit sums add to $36$ for each of 5000 pairs, total $180{,}000$. Plus 1 for $10000$.

**Answer: (A)**

amc12-ahsme-1970-34.title: Differences
amc12-ahsme-1970-34.body:
Same remainder means the divisor divides the differences $13903-13511=392=2^3\cdot7^2$ and $14589-13903=686=2\cdot7^3$. $\gcd(392,686)=2\cdot49=98$.

**Answer: (C) 98**

amc12-ahsme-1970-35.title: Square the equations
amc12-ahsme-1970-35.body:
Pension $P=k\sqrt y$. Then $k^2(y+a)=(P+p)^2$ and $k^2y=P^2$ give $k^2a=2Pp+p^2$; similarly $k^2b=2Pq+q^2$. Eliminate $k^2$: $b(2Pp+p^2)=a(2Pq+q^2)$, so $2P(bp-aq)=aq^2-bp^2$ and
$$P=\frac{aq^2-bp^2}{2(bp-aq)}.$$

**Answer: (D)**
